newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak court rules deputy wrongly stripped of seat.
newsitem.headline: Slovak court rules deputy wrongly stripped of seat.

text.p: Slovakia's Constitutional Court, in a case closely watched by western democracies, ruled on Friday that the Slovak parliament had violated the constitution by illegally stripping a deputy of his mandate.
But it stopped short of ordering parliament to reinstate Frantisek Gaulieder to the seat he lost last December, saying that it lacked the authority.
Gaulieder lost his seat in a vote backed by the populist three-party ruling coalition led by Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS).
"By adopting a resolution... taking note that Frantisek Gaulieder...had resigned his mandate... parliament violated his constitutional right," the court said in its ruling.
The vote was called on the basis of a letter of resignation from parliament that Gaulieder said he had not written and insisted was a deliberate forgery.
It came just weeks after he had resigned from the HZDS in protest over what he said was the party's increasingly authoritarian ways.
The incident was criticised by the European Union and NATO member countries including the United States as an example of weak democratic reforms in Slovakia.

It has been just one of several reasons cited as why Slovakia was excluded from the first wave of invitations for post-Communist countries to join NATO and why the country has not been recommended for fast-track EU integration.

In its ruling, the court rejected a motion by Gaulieder that his mandate be reinstated, on the grounds that the court had no authority to order an overturn of parliament's original decision, or to force deputies to vote for his reinstatement.
Gaulieder, a founding member of the HZDS, resigned from the party last November saying there was a lack of true democracy in the country, but he vowed to retain his seat in parliament.

Following his resignation from the HZDS, the party demanded that he resign his seat. Gaulieder refused and twice wrote to parliament president Ivan Gasparovic, his former HZDS party colleague, stating he would not give up his mandate.

Gasparovic, however, claimed he had received a third letter signed by Gaulieder stating he wanted to give up his seat and passed it on to the mandate committee whose coalition majority recommended Gaulieder's expulsion from parliament.

President Michal Kovac, an avowed political enemy of Meciar, welcomed the court's ruling and noted this was the 13th time the court had ruled as unconstitutional a decision taken by Meciar's parliamentary majority.
"I expect parliament to respect the ruling of the... court and reinstate Gaulieder to parliament," Kovac said in a statement issued by his office.
HZDS officials were not immediately available to comment on the ruling.
Some opposition politicians expressed their doubts that parliament would reverse its decision on Gaulieder's expulsion.

"As I know the coalition deputies they will seek every way to prevent Gaulieder from returning to parliament," Bela Bugar, head of the Hungarian Christian Democratic Movement (MKDH), told the independent SITA news agency.
Gaulieder has also petitioned the European Human Rights Commission in Strasbourg to review his case.
